title: Extremal optimization
summary:
Extremal optimization (EO) is an optimization heuristic inspired by the Bak-Sneppen model of self-organized criticality from the field of statistical physics. This heuristic was designed initially to address combinatorial optimization problems such as the travelling salesman problem and spin glasses.

It was the evolutionary self-organised criticality model by Bak and Sneppen and the observation of critical points in combinatorial optimisation problems that led to the development of Extremal Optimization by Stefan Boettcher and Allon Percus. Unlike genetic algorithms, which work with a population of candidate solutions, EO evolves a single solution and makes local modifications to the worst components. This requires that a suitable representation be selected which permits individual solution components to be assigned a quality measure or fitness.

Graphing holistic solution quality over time shows periods of improvement followed by quality crashes (avalanches), very much in the manner described by punctuated equilibrium. It is these crashes or dramatic jumps in the search space that permit the algorithm to escape local optima and differentiate this approach from other local search procedures. Although such punctuated-equilibrium behaviour can be designed or hard-coded, this is an emergent effect of the negative-component-selection principle fundamental to the algorithm.

EO has primarily been applied to combinatorial problems such as graph partitioning and the travelling salesman problem, as well as problems from statistical physics such as spin glasses. Extensions include Generalised Extremal Optimization (GEO), which operates on bit strings where component quality is determined by the absolute rate of change of the bit, and Continuous Extremal Optimization (CEO). EO has also been applied to image rasterization, used as a local search after ant colony optimization, used to identify structures in complex networks, and applied to multiple target tracking problems.
